readme.intro: One person signs the limits; hundreds or thousands of AI agents trade under them and share one daily budget. The costly orders often break no rule on their own: a position split across agents into slices just under the cap, a runaway loop of small legal orders, a colluding group draining the budget honest agents need. OrderGuard sits between the agents and the money: code enforces the signed limits at a trusted price, a risk model catches the bad flow that fits them, and people review only the orders most likely to cost money.

text.t: This release runs against simulated markets, recorded public market data and paper ledgers. Connecting a live venue is an adapter on top of the receiver, which is already the single path to the ledger.

Every result here was produced on one laptop with a small model budget: live model trials used one low-cost model family, the red-team campaign ran all 336 planned rounds with two cheap attacker models, and the heaviest million-agent simulation materialised 616,500 orders per arm (3 seeds, 12.9 million authority decisions) for one scenario; the other scenarios run at 10,000 agents. Each document states its sample sizes; larger runs are a matter of compute and budget, and every runner takes the scale as a parameter.
OrderGuard has no affiliation with any brokerage or exchange.
